de21_gao.topic: GAO-26-108615 on DOGE's Wall of Receipts savings

claims.text: GAO reviewed $110.34bn of savings DOGE reported on its Wall of Receipts for contracts, grants and leases as of 7 July 2026; DOGE reported total savings of $215bn including other categories.

Contracts: $61.02bn reported across 13,476 contracts; 2,503 contracts representing $27.4bn in reported savings had no termination action in FPDS (GAO notes USAID records may overstate this share); 43.2% of reported contract savings is associated with contracts completely or partially terminated.

DOGE's stated method (total contract value including options minus amount obligated) was followed for only 27.5% of reported contract savings ($16.8bn); for 60.7% ($37.0bn) DOGE used other calculations or the method could not be determined.
Grants: $49.21bn reported across 15,887 grants; for 13,553 grants, $47.32bn or 96.2% of reported grant savings, GAO could not verify the method; DOGE 'did not provide sufficient information'.
Leases: reported as $113.00M but the listed 264 leases sum to $53.5M; 108 leases worth about $15.3M were already in process for termination before DOGE was established.
A $1.7bn reported saving on a Defense Health Agency IT services contract was not a saving: 'no action was taken to terminate the contract, or to reduce scope, value, or funding'.

DOGE did not respond to GAO's requests for information or interviews and the U.S. DOGE Service provided no comments; GAO recommended the EOP, through USDS, prominently display known data-quality issues on the Wall of Receipts.

GAO said deobligated funds 'could reduce federal spending or be spent on higher priority agency needs' but savings are not certain and may be offset if funds are reused; the report does not address the deficit.

de21_dividend.topic: The DOGE dividend proposal and its fate

claims.text: James Fishback, CEO of Azoria Partners, posted a four-page memo on X on 18 February 2025 proposing a 'DOGE dividend': 20% of DOGE savings, which he put at $400bn from a $2 trillion total, sent as $5,000 checks to tax-paying households after DOGE's scheduled end in July 2026; Musk replied 'Will check with the President'.

Speaking in Miami on 19 February 2025 at a meeting hosted by Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund (FII Priority), Trump said a 'new concept' of giving 20% of DOGE savings to citizens and 20% to paying down debt was 'under consideration'; on Air Force One he said 'I love it'.
Reuters' analysis of DOGE's partial data at the time found its contract cuts saved $8.5bn; Musk called $2 trillion a 'best-case outcome' with $1 trillion the goal.
Fishback used $2 trillion in savings and about 78 million tax-paying households to reach about $5,000 per household; the remainder would go to debt.

Speaker Mike Johnson at CPAC 2025: 'Politically, that would be great for us... because everybody gets a check' but 'I think we need to pay down the credit card'; Reps. Celeste Maloy and Riley Moore preferred deficit reduction; Congress would have to decide.

Johnson first said he would be 'happy' to consider it 'once we balance the budget'; Senator Tillis preferred paying down debt, Senator Hawley wanted the savings for a child tax credit; enacting it would need an act of Congress. Musk later said it was 'entirely up to' the president.
A J.L. Partners poll of 1,001 registered voters (24–25 Feb 2025) found 67% supported the $5,000 checks (46% strongly).

de21_end.topic: DOGE's end, what persisted, Musk's later view

claims.text: EO 14158: 'The U.S. DOGE Service Temporary Organization shall terminate on July 4, 2026.' The White House did not say whether DOGE would formally fold; USDS 'appears here to stay'; the April 2026 budget sought $35M for USDS; a House appropriations report directs 'the Administrator of DOGE' to submit quarterly reports on hires, detailees and transfers.

Amy Gleason, acting USDS administrator, leads a health technology office at CMS and said USDS is 'largely continuing that same mission' as the U.S. Digital Service; Joe Gebbia is chief design officer of the National Design Studio reporting to Susie Wiles; Zachary Terrell and Edward Coristine moved to the NDS.
In December 2025 on the Katie Miller Podcast Musk said DOGE was 'a little bit successful' and that he would not do it again, preferring to have worked at his companies.
In November 2025 OPM Director Scott Kupor told Reuters DOGE 'doesn't exist'; he later wrote on X that DOGE 'may not have centralized leadership' but 'the principles of DOGE remain alive and well'.
DOGE's savings page had not been updated since 1 January 2026 and claimed $215bn, $1,335.40 per taxpayer; about 140,000 employees opted into deferred resignation per OPM data from May 2026.

At a House Appropriations Financial Services subcommittee hearing on 30 June 2026 OMB Director Russell Vought said 'We have no plans to do kind of a closing DOGE report' and that 'the fruits of their labor are sprinkled all across the government'.

FNN reported that DOGE.gov had gone offline, that some former senior DOGE officials held permanent federal posts, that USDS had shifted toward citizen-services projects, and that some agencies such as the Nuclear Regulatory Commission had begun rehiring.

At his Oval Office farewell on 30 May 2025 Musk said 'This is not the end of DOGE. It's really just the beginning'; Trump gave him a golden key; the DOGE website then estimated $175bn in savings and Musk still expected $1 trillion over time.
On 21 September 2025 at Charlie Kirk's memorial Musk sat beside Trump, shook hands and talked, posting a photo captioned 'For Charlie'; Trump said 'I thought it was nice that he came over'.

Musk, November 2024: 'There should be no need for FOIA requests. All government data should be default public for maximum transparency'; 11 February 2025: 'all of our actions are maximally transparent' and 'I don't know of a case where an organization has been more transparent than the DOGE organization'.
In a filing on 27 February 2025 in CREW's FOIA suit, DOJ argued that after 20 January 2025 USDS left OMB and became a standalone EOP component: 'As a result, USDS is not subject to FOIA.'

GAO identified 206 DOGE personnel in EOP positions from 20 January 2025 to 31 January 2026, four characterized as leaders, 27 SGEs; at least 128 had left by 31 January 2026; EOP did not respond to GAO's requests for training records and financial disclosures; nine agencies reported on 64 DOGE personnel (49 completed ethics training, 38 filed financial disclosures); ten agencies did not provide information timely or at all; the temporary organization within USDS terminated on 4 July 2026.

de21_conflicts.topic: Musk companies, regulators and contracts during and after DOGE

claims.text: Democratic staff of the Senate PSI counted 65 active or potential enforcement actions involving Musk's companies across 11 agencies, quantified 40 at $2.37bn potential liability ('a credible, conservative estimate'), 25 unquantified; examples: FAA (SpaceX launch requirements), NHTSA Tesla self-driving probes, Neuralink animal welfare, DOJ dismissal of the SpaceX discrimination suit, Autopilot statements, union retaliation; companies gave 'abjectly inadequate cooperation'.

On 20 February 2025 DOJ asked the Southern District of Texas to lift the stay so it could dismiss with prejudice its 2023 suit alleging SpaceX discouraged asylees and refugees from applying; the case had been paused since November 2023 by a challenge to DOJ's administrative authority; SpaceX denied wrongdoing; no reason given.

On 7 October 2025 NHTSA opened an investigation covering 2,882,566 Teslas with FSD after 58 reports of traffic-law violations; it had opened a probe into late crash reporting in August 2025, and other probes (Summon; 2.4M vehicles low-visibility) were ongoing.

FAA proposed $633,009 in civil penalties against SpaceX on 17 September 2024 for using an unapproved control room and skipping a readiness poll (18 June 2023) and using an unapproved propellant farm (28 July 2023).
Musk called the FAA's proposed penalty 'more lawfare' and wrote 'SpaceX will be filing suit against the FAA for regulatory overreach' (17 September 2024).

Musk wrote of FAA Administrator Mike Whitaker on 25 September 2024 'He needs to resign'; Whitaker announced on 12 December 2024 he would resign and left on 20 January 2025 after about 15 months of a five-year term; Snopes found no evidence Musk pushed him out.

In February–March 2025 the FAA tested Starlink terminals in Alaska and at Oklahoma City and Atlantic City under an L3Harris contract; SpaceX said kits were leased 'free-of-charge' and denied any effort to 'take over' Verizon's 15-year $2.4bn 2023 contract; Duffy said Starlink was 'part of a solution'; three SpaceX engineers received DOT ethics waivers to serve as SGEs at the FAA.
In December 2025 DOT and FAA named Peraton prime integrator for the air-traffic-control overhaul with $12.5bn from the One Big Beautiful Bill; Starlink and SpaceX were not mentioned.

On 19 August 2025 the Fifth Circuit in Space Exploration Technologies Corp. v. NLRB held the NLRB's structure likely unconstitutional (removal protections of members and ALJs) and affirmed preliminary injunctions barring unfair-labour-practice proceedings against SpaceX and two other employers.

On 9 May 2025 Trump signed S.J.Res. 28 repealing the CFPB's November 2024 larger-participant supervision rule for large nonbank 'general-use digital consumer payment applications', and S.J.Res. 18 repealing the overdraft rule.
On 28 January 2025 X CEO Linda Yaccarino announced X Money, a payments service with Visa as first partner.

On 25 September 2025 GSA announced a OneGov agreement making xAI's Grok 4 models available to federal agencies at $0.42 per agency for 18 months to March 2027, calling it the 'final frontier model' added to GSA's AI offerings.

The SEC sued Musk in January 2025 alleging he missed a 2022 deadline to disclose a 5% Twitter stake, costing shareholders more than $150M; in December 2024 SEC attorneys had asked him to pay more than $200M; the case settled for $1.5M, which an SEC spokesperson called a record for late disclosure and Musk's lawyer called a 'small fine'; Judge Sparkle Sooknanan approved it in July 2026 'despite its significant misgivings', having said in May the deal raised 'red flags' including whether Musk received 'special treatment'; her order said the court 'may not step in the shoes of the SEC'.
On 5 February 2025 press secretary Karoline Leavitt said that if Musk found a conflict with contracts and funding DOGE oversaw, 'Elon will excuse himself from those contracts'.

de21_claims.topic: DOGE public claims against the record

claims.text: In the Oval Office in February 2025 Musk said Social Security records included people '150 years old' and posted screenshots of millions marked alive; a 2023 SSA inspector general report had found nearly 19 million people born before 1920 with no death information in Numident, which SSA chose not to fix because of cost; economists Kathleen Romig and Justin Wolfers said the claim misread the data.
Acting SSA Commissioner Lee Dudek said on 20 February 2025 that people aged 100 and over with no recorded date of death 'are not necessarily receiving benefits'.
Musk: 'Nobody's going to bat a thousand. We will make mistakes, but we'll act quickly to correct any mistakes.'

The NYT reported that DOGE's Wall of Receipts listed an $8bn ICE contract that was worth $8M; three $655M USAID cuts that were one cut counted three times (now $18M); a $232M SSA cut that was a $560,000 project; and a $1.9bn Treasury cut made under Biden; DOGE said it 'always used the correct $8M in its calculations'.

de21_book3.topic: Audit record used in Book III's closing test

claims.text: Four agencies (CFPB, Education, NOAA, SEC) reported DOGE teams had access to more than 23 systems (19 at CFPB); SBA and VA did not identify their systems; the 'extent and level of access' could not be determined; CFPB, Education, SEC, NOAA and VA declined or limited cooperation, some questioning GAO's authority; Congress and the public 'lack information needed to confirm if DOGE team members followed the IT rules'.

The workforce of 22 agencies 'declined by nearly 256,000 employees—or more than 11 percent' from December 2024 to January 2026; nearly 378,000 separated in 2025 and about 127,000 were hired; about 65% of separations came in the second half of the year.

Cavalcanti, Rasella et al. (The Lancet, 2025) combined a 2001–2021 retrospective analysis of 133 countries (USAID support associated with a 15% reduction in all-cause mortality) with microsimulation forecasts, projecting that 'more than 14 million additional deaths could occur by 2030, including over 4.5 million among children under five' if the cuts continue: a model projection, not a count.

The Supreme Court agreed to hear U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for D.C. (No. 25-1103), CREW's FOIA case, with argument expected early 2027; Judge Cooper had found USDS 'likely an agency subject to FOIA'; on its emergency docket the Court had earlier held the discovery order too broad without deciding FOIA status; the administration argues USDS 'does not exercise independent authority' and that agency DOGE teams 'operate under each agency's authority, not USDS'.
